\[ P(5 \text{ or } 6 \text{ or } 9) = \frac{4 + 5 + 4}{36} = \frac{13}{36} \approx .36 \]
Nothing else on this board gets past \(10/36\), or about .28. The board had some clues: the red numbers, the 6s and 8s, are individually the most likely totals (since there’s no 7 on this board; in the real game something else happens when 7 is rolled). But a settlement’s probability depends on all the different totals that pay it. The little dots on the tokens were another clue: they count how many of the 36 outcomes produce that total. To find the probability of any intersection on this board, add the dots on the tiles it touches and divide by 36.
Of course, just picking the best spot in a statistical sense won’t win you the game. Like we pointed out already, a probability of about \(.36\) does not guarantee that those three numbers will occur on exactly 36 out of 100 real rolls. In a single game of Catan, any given corner might pay out more or less than expected.2 But at least now you can reason about your choice in a precise way.

title: 6  Probability
text:
Probability and Distributions of Scores
The same logic applies to the scores we study in social science. We can ask for the probability of randomly selecting a score equal to a value, above a value, or within a range.
Take this little distribution of ten scores.



Figure 6.6: A block histogram showing a distribution of 10 scores: four 1s, three 2s, two 4s, and one 5.




Block histogram of ten scores: four 1s, three 2s, two 4s, and one 5.





If we select one score at random, each of the ten blocks is one equally likely outcome. Let \(X\) stand for the value of the score we select. Four of the ten blocks have a value of 1, so:
\[ P(X = 1) = \frac{4}{10} = .4 \]
There are no blocks at 3, so \(P(X=3)=0\). And we can define events that collect several values at once:
\[ P(X \ge 4) = \frac{3}{10} = .3 \]
\[ P(1 < X < 5) = \frac{5}{10} = .5 \]
The block histogram describes scores we’ve already observed, but those proportions also tell us what to expect when we randomly select one of the blocks. If we repeatedly select a block at random, putting it back each time, we would expect about 40% of our selections to give a score of 1. Once again, we’re using a distribution to reason about selections we haven’t made yet.
What if we’re interested in a continuous variable, such as height or reaction time, rather than a little collection of scores we can count? Remember the smooth curves in Chapter 2. They represented models of how scores were distributed, including scores we hadn’t actually observed. We called the height density back in Chapter 2. A high part of the curve means scores are concentrated around that value, but the density itself isn’t a probability. We scale the curve so that its total area is 1. Computing the area between two scores then gives the probability of a randomly selected score falling within that interval.3



Figure 6.7: A smoothed curve like the ones we saw in Chapter 2. The shaded region between scores of 2 and 3 contains about 30% of the total area.




A smooth density curve with the region between scores of 2 and 3 shaded, containing about 30% of the total area.





For the curve in Figure 6.7, which you might recognize from Chapter 2, about 30% of its area lies between 2 and 3. That means a randomly selected score from that modeled distribution has about a .30 probability of falling within that range. Of course, the math behind that answer depends on the precise contours of that curve: a different shape would produce different probabilities. That’s why I mentioned back in Chapter 2 that one curve in particular would become very important to us: the normal curve.

title: 6  Probability
text:
The Normal Distribution
The normal distribution is so useful to us because its entire shape is determined by just two numbers: the mean and the standard deviation. Those two features are enough to determine probabilities under a normal model.



Figure 6.8: A normal curve, representing a simple model of a population of scores.




A symmetrical bell-shaped normal curve representing a hypothetical population of scores.





Okay, the math that defines the curve is more involved than I’m making it sound. Here’s the equation:
\[Y = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2}} e^{-\frac{(X-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}} \tag{6.1}\]
You don’t really have to know this equation for the work we’re going to do throughout this book, so if it makes you sweat just looking at it, don’t worry. But it is worth looking at briefly to get a sense of how it’s constructed. The value \(Y\) gives the height of the curve (its density) at a particular value of \(X\) (which is part of the exponent over to the right). You can find both the parameters, \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\), along with some other constants like \(e\) and \(\pi\). But again, don’t worry about remembering the specifics. Just know that the equation defines the curve precisely, its shape is entirely determined by the mean and standard deviation, and it gives us a curve with a total area of 1, so we can read its areas as probabilities in exactly the way we just described.
Continuing with the historical theme of games of chance, this was figured out in large part by French mathematician Abraham de Moivre, while thinking about the long-run probabilities of simple events with two equally-likely outcomes, like a coin toss. Like we saw earlier, for a fair coin, each outcome (heads or tails) has a probability of \(.5\). But what happens when you toss a coin a bunch of times, say 3,600? Will you get precisely half—1,800—come up heads? Probably not. Toss the coin another 3,600 times and you’ll get a different answer again. If you had the time to do this over and over again, the answers would usually be somewhere close to the expected 1,800; occasionally (but rarely) would it be far away.
De Moivre realized that we can approximate the distribution of all these possible outcomes with a simple smooth curve—the normal distribution. He calculated that the distribution was centered at 1,800 and had a spread equivalent to what we would now call a standard deviation of 30. Using his normal curve, De Moivre worked out that if we were to flip a coin 3,600 times, there was about a 68% chance of getting between 1,770 and 1,830 heads (Moivre, 1738, Corollary 4). In other words, .68 of the area under the curve is in the region between those values.



Figure 6.9: A normal approximation for the number of heads in 3,600 fair coin flips. The shaded region, from 1,770 to 1,830 heads, contains about 68% of the total area.




Normal approximation for the number of heads in 3,600 fair coin flips, with mean 1,800 and standard deviation 30. The shaded region from 1,770 to 1,830 contains about 68% of the area.






The Unit Normal Table
This math works for a normal distribution with any mean and standard deviation, but it is often easiest to work with the standard normal distribution, also called the unit normal distribution. This is a normal distribution with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1. Sound familiar? We described standardizing distributions using \(z\)-scores in exactly this way in Chapter 5. For a normally distributed variable, that transformation gives us this standard normal distribution.
So now we can determine areas under the curve and interpret them as the probability of a randomly selected score falling in that region. So, for example, 34.13% of the area of the curve lies between the mean and one standard deviation above the mean. Because it’s symmetrical, the same 34.13% lies between the mean and one standard deviation below the mean. Another 13.59% lies between one and two standard deviations from the mean on each side. And 2.28% lies more than two standard deviations above the mean, with another 2.28% more than two standard deviations below it. Together, the two extreme regions contain about 4.56% of the distribution.



Figure 6.10: Percentages of the standard normal distribution in each region between \(z=-2\), \(z=-1\), \(z=0\), \(z=1\), and \(z=2\).




Standard normal curve divided at z = -2, -1, 0, 1, and 2, with each region labeled by the percentage of the distribution it contains: 2.28%, 13.59%, 34.13%, 34.13%, 13.59%, and 2.28%.





Of course, we aren’t limited to whole-number \(z\)-scores. We can take any \(z\)-score and determine the probability of a score falling above or below that value under a standard normal model. In the olden days, you would look up something called a \(z\) table, a standard normal table, or a unit normal table. (Computers have made these tables largely obsolete, but it’s useful for us to see how they work, because whatever statistical software you might use in practice is applying the same logic and math.) These tables vary in how they’re arranged. The one below lists nonnegative \(z\) scores along with the areas to their left, to their right, and between the mean and the score.



Table 6.2: The unit normal table, showing areas to the left, right, and between the mean and a given \(z\) score. Scroll to see more values.




Unit normal table showing areas to the left, right, and between the mean and z.





So for a \(z\) score of zero, it’s exactly half and half; 50 percent of the distribution lies on either side of zero, because zero is the mean and the distribution is symmetrical. In other words, under a normal model there is a 50 percent chance of observing a score greater than the mean and a 50 percent chance of observing a score lower than the mean.
If we take a \(z\) score of 1, we look for that row in the table. The area to the left of \(z=1\) is about .84, so roughly 84 percent of the distribution lies below it. In percentile language, a score with \(z=1\) is at about the 84th percentile. The area to the right is just under .16, and the area between the mean (where \(z=0\)) and \(z=1\) is .3413, just like we saw before. How about a \(z\) score of negative one? Standard normal tables don’t always list negative \(z\) scores, because the symmetry of the distribution means the relevant areas are the same as for a positive \(z\) score on the opposite side of the mean. Only the direction flips: the smaller area (0.1587) is to the left of \(z = -1\) and the larger area (0.8413) is to its right.
What if we want the area between two scores, such as \(z=0.5\) and \(z=1.5\)? Subtract the area to the left of \(0.5\) from the area to the left of \(1.5\), leaving just the interval between them:
\[P(0.5 < z < 1.5) = .9332 - .6915 = .2417\]
So about 24.17% of scores in a standard normal distribution fall in that interval.

title: 6  Probability
text:
Applying Probability: Spider-Man
To finish up, let’s turn back to our Spider-Man reaction time test from the previous chapter. We found that Peter Parker’s \(z\) score was \(-1.9\), and we said that that seemed pretty extreme. If we model the distribution of reaction times as a normal distribution, as we assumed in Chapter 5, we’re now equipped to be more precise.
What are the chances that if we randomly selected someone from our reference population of ordinary, unbitten people they would have a reaction time as quick as Peter’s or quicker? As you can see on the normal curve, reaction times that fast make up a very small lower-tail region of the distribution.



Figure 6.11: A normal distribution curve with a vertical line at \(z = -1.9\), representing the position of Peter Parker’s reaction time within the standardized population distribution.




Standard normal curve with a vertical line at z equals negative 1.9 and the small region below it shaded.





Our table lists positive \(z\)-scores, so look up \(1.9\) and read the area to its right. By symmetry, this is also the area to the left of \(-1.9\): about .0287, or 2.87%:
\[P(z \le -1.9) \approx .0287\]
In other words, under our assumed model, if we tested a random individual from this population, there’s less than a 3% chance that they would be as quick as or quicker than Peter Parker. So we might interpret that rarity as evidence against the idea that Peter is just an ordinary member of the reference population. It isn’t proof. People with very fast reaction times do exist: we just said they make up around 3% of the population, after all. So the 3% shouldn’t be interpreted as the probability that the spider bite changed Parker. Rather it suggests that either the spider bite did nothing and we just happened to see a very fast reaction time by chance, or perhaps it did cause a change and Parker doesn’t belong to that population. In Chapter 8, we’ll develop that logic into a formal hypothesis test.

A Note on Normality
One last thing to be clear: the probabilities in the unit normal table only apply to the precise mathematical normal distribution. If the population distribution has a different shape (skewed, bimodal, or something like that) the normal curve’s areas will not apply. Remember that converting raw scores into \(z\)-scores is just a change of label. It won’t turn a nonnormal distribution into a normal one. So in practice we need to be sure that the normal distribution is a reasonable model for the data we’re working with and for what we’re trying to do with it. In the next chapter we’ll start examining the distribution of sample statistics, like the mean. And we’ll see that, luckily for us, a distribution of sample means can be approximately normal even when the population the samples come from is not.

title: 7  Sampling
text:
The Quincunx
In the previous chapter, we used the normal distribution to determine the probability of seeing individual scores within a given range. But researchers usually collect a sample and summarize its scores with a statistic, like the mean. In Chapter 4, we saw that sample means vary because of sampling error, even though their errors balance out in the long run. Now we’ll ask how widely those means vary, and which results would be surprising.
Before we proceed, take a moment to enjoy this little toy. (It’s a digital version of a real thing you can buy and keep on your desk to turn to in moments of boredom.)
It’s called a Galton board, after Francis Galton, who developed it in the 1870s. (Galton also called it the Quincunx, meaning five points, as in the arrangement of groups of pegs.) The physical version is a little box with a clear front, rows of pegs, and lots of little balls (originally lead shot, like from shotgun pellets; ammunition manufacturers by this time were able to make the precise, uniform spheres that the demonstration requires).
As Galton inscribed on the original device, when set upright on a level table, “the shot will all drop into the funnel, and running thence through its mouth, will pursue devious courses through the harrow and will accumulate in the vertical compartments at the bottom, there affording a representation of the law of dispersion.”
By “law of dispersion,” Galton meant the tendency for the balls to end up in a predictable distribution—this is the same approximation of the normal distribution that Abraham de Moivre had discovered by thinking about a random process like flipping a coin many times. Each individual ball’s course is unpredictable, but the aggregate of all those “devious courses” looks roughly the same each time.1
In our digital board, each ball encounters twelve pegs, with an independent 50/50 chance of bouncing left or right at each one. To end up in the far-left slot, it has to bounce left every time. There is only one way for that to happen, just like there’s only one way to roll two dice and get a total of two. To land in the middle, a ball needs to take six lefts and six rights, and there are many different sequences that produce that mix, just like there are many ways to roll a seven with the pair of dice. We can’t predict any one ball’s path, but we can describe the pattern of possible landing places.

title: 7  Sampling
text:
Sampling Error
Our purpose in this chapter is to understand how sampling from a population works—how we can quantify our trust in a sample as a fair representation of the population it came from. The Quincunx is a nice visual analogy for that process. Imagine that each ball is collecting a sample as it falls through the pegs. Each bounce supplies one observation; the final slot is the sample statistic, summarizing all twelve observations.
Let’s make the analogy more concrete with political opinion polling. Say support for Candidate Left and Candidate Right is split exactly 50/50 in the population. If we select twelve people at random, sampling error means we won’t necessarily find six supporters of each. Seven and five wouldn’t be too surprising. Or even 8 and 4. We could even get twelve supporters of Candidate Left, like a Quincunx ball bouncing left twelve times in a row. It’s unlikely, but not impossible. Repeat the poll over and over with different samples of twelve people each time and the results would form a distribution like the pile on the Galton board: results near 50% support would be common, while results near 0% or 100% would be rare.
Which poll would surprise you more?Imagine two polls drawn at random from our evenly split population.
One asks 12 people, the other asks 1,200. Which would surprise you more
if three-quarters of its respondents supported Candidate Left? Why? Try

surprising.ExplanationNeither result is impossible. The question is how much room chance
has to produce a lop-sided result when the population itself is evenly
split.
What if we had a sample of 100 people, rather than 12? In this case we’d expect something like 50 people to support each candidate, but it wouldn’t be too surprising if we saw something like 55/45. It would be surprising if we happened to get 100 people who all support Candidate Left. Now what if our sample size was 1,000? Or 1,000,000? Your intuition is probably telling you that the larger the sample, the more surprising an extremely lop-sided result would be.
This is, in effect, what the error bars on graphs of opinion poll results convey. (The precise math behind the margin of error is something we’ll talk more about in Chapter 10.) The error bars express uncertainty about population support around each estimate, allowing for sampling error.

Notice that the two polls put different candidates ahead, but the gaps are small compared with the uncertainty around each estimate. As Pew put it, “the contest is so close that we cannot confidently predict the winner of the popular vote.” The actual popular vote was 47.9% for Bush and 48.4% for Gore, both within these polls’ margins of error. Sampling variability and people changing their minds or withholding opinions complicate what a poll can tell us.

Sampling Error with IQ Scores
The opinion poll results summarize categorical responses with a proportion. Now we’ll turn to quantitative data. What would happen if we could repeatedly take samples from a population and summarize each sample with a quantitative statistic like the mean?
Say we have a population with normally distributed IQ scores, a mean of 100, and a standard deviation of 15. We randomly collect ten observations, find their mean, then draw another ten and repeat. We did this kind of thing in Activity 4.3 in Chapter 4. There, we tracked the samples’ errors and saw their average approach zero. This time we’ll collect the means themselves into a block histogram, to see which occur most often and how widely they vary as they pile up.






Activity 7.1: Build the sampling distribution





Interactive pathway from an IQ population through samples to a distribution of sample means.




We start with the normally distributed IQ population, where \(\mu=100\) and \(\sigma=15\). As usual, this population is fixed; its characteristics don’t change while we sample from it.


Now we select ten observations at random from the population.


Next we compute the sample mean: the balance point for this particular set of 10 observations. The blue block marks this sample mean (\(M =\) ...) on the sample’s IQ-score axis.


We want to keep track of every sample mean we obtain, so now that mean block drops down onto the lower Distribution of sample means tracker. As we collect more means, this will become a kind of block histogram.


Now we can take a second sample. It produces a different mean block, which drops down. The sample means are different even though the population hasn’t changed. Each mean’s difference from the population mean of 100 is that sample’s sampling error.


Now we just keep repeating the process. Each sample converges into a blue mean block, which joins the growing pile. After thirty samples, there isn’t much of a pattern. But thirty isn’t very many in the grand scheme of things: we need more.


Let’s speed things up a bit. Each tick we get a new sample of 10 individual scores, from which we compute a new sample mean. After collecting 200 samples, a pattern is becoming evident. The distribution of means piles up around the true population mean in a roughly symmetrical distribution. Most sample means are near 100, and extreme ones are rare. The spread of the distribution of means is less than that of the original population.




Notice how similar the final shape of the histogram of sample means in Activity 7.1 is to the shape of the balls at the bottom of the Quincunx. The process is different; instead of balls randomly bouncing off pegs, we are randomly selecting members of the population. But the reason for the outcome is similar: when we sample randomly from a population, there are lots of ways for a sample mean to be close to the true population mean, but few ways for it to be very far away.
The name for the kind of distribution we created is a distribution of sample means, or sampling distribution of the mean. And the predictability of its shape is the key insight that powers the inferential statistics we’ll begin using in the next chapter.

title: 7  Sampling
text:
The Distribution of Sample Means
Technically the sampling distribution of the mean is the distribution of sample means obtained by selecting all possible samples of a given sample size \(n\) from a population. For the IQ distribution, we ended with 200 random samples, not every possible sample. As you might imagine, for any reasonably large population, there’s often a huge number of possible samples; for practical purposes, the number might be effectively infinite. We’ll return to this problem shortly, but we won’t let it stop us from demonstrating the fundamental principles now. We just need a small, manageable population, from which we can obtain all possible samples of a given size. Like, very small.
Suppose we have a population consisting of just four people. We’re interested in their height. We have one person 60 inches tall, one 62, one 64, and one 66.

This slightly tedious process has given us a new kind of population: the set of every sample mean. We can describe its characteristics just as we would for any other population.
We can, for example, figure out its mean. The mean of the distribution of sample means is called the expected value of the mean, \(\mu_M\). Its value should be obvious visually. We can also calculate the standard deviation of the 16 means. The standard deviation of the sampling distribution is also called the standard error of the mean. The symbol for this is \(\sigma_M\). We can calculate it in the same way we did in Chapter 4, by putting all those values in a table, working out columns for deviations, the squared deviations, then using those to get the sum of squared deviations, the variance, and the standard deviation. title: 7  Sampling
text:
The Central Limit Theorem
The trouble with distributions of sample means is that it’s just not feasible in most realistic situations to obtain every possible sample of a given size for a population. Listing every possible sample worked for four people and samples of two. But imagine doing that for, say, all American voters. Even if we knew everyone’s scores, the number of possible samples would be astronomical. (Also, if we knew everyone’s scores, we wouldn’t need to sample anyway.)
Thankfully, some simple equations and a theorem can help. We can predict the sampling distribution’s characteristics without compiling every possible sample. Its center and variability follow from the population mean, population variability, and sample size, and the Central Limit Theorem tells us about its shape.5

Center: The Expected Value of the Mean
The center of the sampling distribution is simple: the average of all the sample means equals the population mean. This is because \(M\) is an unbiased statistic: some of the sample means are above the true population mean, some are below, and they balance out perfectly. So the expected value of the mean is exactly equal to the population mean:
\[\mu_M = \mu \tag{7.1}\]
For our four heights, both the population mean and the mean of all 16 sample means were 63. It wasn’t a coincidence! It reflects the sample mean’s lack of bias.


Variability: The Standard Error of the Mean
Unlike its center, the variability of the sampling distribution (its standard error, \(\sigma_M\)) is not equal to the population variability. Instead it is smaller, as a function of the sample size, \(n\).
\[\sigma_M = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \tag{7.2}\]
The numerator is the population standard deviation, \(\sigma\). So the larger the variability in the population, the larger the standard error of the mean. The denominator is the square root of the sample size. And so the larger our sample size, the smaller the standard error of the mean.
An algebraically equivalent form is useful if you have variance, \(\sigma^2\), rather than the standard deviation, \(\sigma\):
\[\sigma_M = \dfrac{\sqrt{\sigma^2}}{\sqrt{n}} \tag{7.3}\]
You can see how they are equivalent: \(\sigma^2\) is literally just \(\sigma\) squared, so \(\sqrt{\sigma^2}\) is the same as \(\sigma\).
Returning to our toy population of heights, we can figure out the standard error of the mean using just known population characteristics. Remember, we said the standard deviation of the population of four heights is \(\sigma = 2.24\). So if we put it into that equation, we get:
\[\sigma_M = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{2.24}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 1.58\]
It’s the same answer as when we went through the full rigmarole of compiling all possible samples for that little population and computing their standard deviation manually! Plugging two numbers into an equation could have saved us a lot of work there.
Of course, the real value is applying the equation where we couldn’t compile all possible samples to double-check the answer. Let’s return to IQ scores and see how sample size affects the standard error.






ActivitySee how sample size affects the standard error





Dashed normal population curve with mean 100 and standard deviation 15; a blue sampling distribution changes width as sample size varies from 2 to 30, on fixed axes.




Here’s a normal curve representing a population’s IQ distribution, with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15. The dashed curve represents the density of individual scores.


The blue curve shows the distribution of sample means for \(n = 10\). Like the population, it has a mean of 100, but its variability is lower. The standard error is \(15/\sqrt{10} \approx 4.74\). In the population, scores lower than 90, for example, are not too uncommon, but sample means lower than 90 are very rare.


If we reduce the sample size to five the blue curve gets wider and flatter. The standard error has increased: \(15 / \sqrt{5} \approx 6.71\). Means from smaller samples vary more widely. Compared with the \(n = 10\) distribution, sample means lower than 90 are more common in this distribution.


Now let’s increase the sample size to \(n = 30\). The standard error falls to about 2.74, and the curve gets narrower and taller. Now there’s almost no chance of seeing a sample mean lower than 90. The larger the sample size, the more tightly clustered the sample means are around the population mean.


Drag the slider to try different sample sizes, and watch how the spread of the blue curve and the value of the standard error change, while its center remains the same.






Shape of the Sampling Distribution
It wasn’t a coincidence that the distribution of the Quincunx balls, IQ samples, and height sampling distribution all took on the same basic shape: approximately normal, with most values clustered in the middle with extreme values trailing off symmetrically on either side. (Okay, the heights sampling distribution was more of a triangle, because of the tiny population and sample size, but still in the same ballpark.) The Central Limit Theorem helps explain when we can expect a sampling distribution to be approximately normal.
If the population we’re sampling from is normally distributed, we’re good: its distribution of sample means will be normal, whatever the sample size. But even if the population is not normal, the distribution of means approaches normality as sample size increases. You’ll sometimes hear \(n = 30\) as a rule of thumb for when the distribution of means is “close enough” to normal. But there’s no magic threshold. For a nonnormal population, the distribution of means never becomes exactly normal; the approximation improves gradually, at a rate that depends on the population’s shape. Activity 7.2 lets us see that in action.

We begin again with a normal population on a standardized \(z\)-score scale. As in Activity 7.1, we’ll repeatedly draw samples and collect their means. (It won’t contain every possible mean, just a large, random collection.)


First we can generate just 200 independent samples of \(n=5\) and plot each sample mean. The predicted normal curve is smooth: because the population itself is normal, its distribution of means is normal at every sample size. With only 200 means, the histogram is lumpy, not following exactly the predicted curve. But the observed mean and standard error are very close to the equations’ predictions.


With only 200 means, there’s still a lot of random lumpiness. Let’s increase the total to one million sample means. At a million means, the random bumps mostly settle down, and the observed mean and standard error come very close to the equations’ predictions. More simulations reveal the sampling distribution more precisely.


Now let’s replace the normal population with a strongly right-skewed one, and reset the distribution of means. We’ll do the same thing again for this skewed population, taking many samples and collecting each sample mean on the distribution tracker.


Here come a million independent samples of \(n=5\). Now we’ll keep the same skewed population, but increase each sample to \(n=30\) and generate one million new means. The distribution is narrower again, and now looks much closer to normal. But it’s still not quite perfectly normal.


The difference between the normal curve and the actual distribution is hard to see at this scale, so we can zoom in (without reshaping the data). First I’ll add a second ruler underneath the scores, like we did in Chapter 5. Its center is \(\mu\), and each unit is one standard error, \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\).


Now we stretch the histogram and predicted curve to fill the lower panel. These are the same one million means; only the scale has changed. The remaining asymmetry is easier to see now: \(n=30\) hasn’t flipped a switch that makes the distribution exactly normal.


Now let’s increase sample size again, to \(n=100\), and generate one million new means. We’ll keep the standard-error ruler stretched out so we can compare the shapes more easily. The histogram follows the normal curve even more closely than at \(n = 30\), but the distribution of means still isn’t perfectly normal. The improvement is gradual, with no special boundary at 30 or anywhere else. The approximation may be good enough, but how much remaining nonnormality matters depends on what we use it for.

title: 7  Sampling
text:
Sampling People in Practice
So now we’ve seen a few examples of normality and predictability emerging from random sampling. We’re almost ready to apply these tools in the context of social science research. But first, let’s take a moment to consider how closely collecting data from people resembles the sampling in our demonstrations. The version of the Central Limit Theorem we’ve used assumes independent observations drawn from the same population distribution; applying it in practice requires those assumptions to be reasonable approximations.

Random Selection, Replacement, and Independence
First let’s define three terms. Random sampling is about how we choose observations: we use a chance procedure. Replacement is about whether someone or something already selected can be selected again within the same sample. Independence is about whether knowing one observation changes the probabilities for another.
In the demonstrations above, I sampled with replacement. This was most obvious with the small population of four heights: the 16 possible samples of \(n = 2\) included samples in which the same person appeared twice. To see why that mattered, let’s turn to another statistics textbook favorite: picking marbles out of a jar.
In The Art of Conjecturing, published in 1713, Jacob Bernoulli asked his reader to imagine an urn containing 5,000 pebbles, in some unknown ratio of white to black. By drawing pebbles repeatedly, someone who couldn’t see the contents could estimate that ratio from the proportion of white pebbles they observed (Bernoulli, 2006).
To keep things simple, imagine a jar with just 50 marbles, 40 blue and 10 white. We want to pick out two marbles, one after the other. If each marble is equally likely to be drawn, the probability of white on our first draw is \(P(\text{white})=10/50=.2\).
So far so simple. But what is the probability that a second draw will also be white? To answer that, we need to know a small but important procedural detail: did we put the first marble back, or leave it out?
If we sample with replacement, we put it back and mix the jar before drawing again. There are still 10 white marbles among 50, so the probability stays .2, whatever color we drew first. The draws are independent.
If we sample without replacement, we leave the first marble out. After drawing white, only 9 white marbles and 49 marbles in total remain, so the probability of another white is \(9/49 \approx .184\). After drawing blue, it would instead be \(10/49 \approx .204\). The draws are dependent: knowing the first result changes the probabilities for the second.
Both procedures are random, but only the first gives us independent draws. For people, choosing names by lottery from a complete population list works the same way. Without replacement, this produces a simple random sample: every possible set of \(n\) people has the same chance of being selected. Random doesn’t mean choosing whoever happens to be nearby, and it doesn’t require replacement.


Can We Treat People’s Scores as Independent?
Do you sense a potential problem here? Social scientists study people, who aren’t like marbles we can put back into a jar. Social scientists generally collect data from each participant once. Strictly speaking, this makes successive selections dependent, as it is sampling without replacement. But like the (non)normality of the sampling distribution, the problem is a matter of degree. What matters is the fraction sampled across the whole sample, not just the tiny change after the first draw.
If the sample is only a small fraction of the population, removing those people barely changes who is available. Selecting 100 people randomly from a population of 10,000 removes just 1% of the population in total. The resulting dependence is weak enough that treating the observations as independent is a good enough approximation. If we sampled a much bigger chunk of those 10,000 people, say 5,000, sampling without replacement would noticeably reduce the variability of the sampling distribution. The usual formula, \(\sigma_M=\sigma/\sqrt{n}\), would fail to account for that reduction and would therefore overstate the standard error.6
Still, would allowing someone to participate twice—sampling with replacement—be better? Usually not. Dependence can come in other forms. In our height example, sampling with replacement gives independent draws of the heights. But for other kinds of research, participating in a study can change someone: they may learn the task or remember the questions. Selecting them again doesn’t make them naive to the procedure, so their second score would not be independent of their first. In that case, sampling without replacement is better, even if it introduces a small amount of dependence across the sample.
Dependence can also arise among different people. Responses from members of one household may share influences; pupils in one classroom share a teacher and learning environment. An opinion poll sampling whole households could underestimate the standard error if it treated all their responses as independent. Studies that do things like that can still be useful, but their analysis needs to account for dependence. (Sometimes we deliberately measure people before and after a treatment, for example. Those paired responses are related, so we need an analysis that accounts for that, which we’ll see in Chapter 13.)


Which Population Are We Sampling?
Lastly, we should point out that even if we are appropriately ensuring independence in a statistical sense, we still need to be careful that our sample is a fair representation of the population we are trying to make inferences about. Remember Köbel’s proposal in Chapter 3 to define a foot by averaging the feet of sixteen men leaving church? Suppose we wanted to estimate the average foot length of the town’s adult men. A simple random sample could happen to include some unusually large feet. That’s sampling error; across repeated random samples, high and low estimates would balance around those men’s mean.
Now imagine trying Köbel’s procedure outside the locker room of the New York Knicks basketball team. We’d probably get a much larger average foot size. Or imagine lining up my kid’s second-grade class: we’d get a much smaller answer. Both procedures systematically favor feet unlike those of the town’s complete population of adult men: that’s selection bias. Even choosing randomly within those niche groups of basketball players or kids wouldn’t fix it.
Somewhat more subtly, say we recruit people for an opinion poll by randomly dialing phone numbers listed in a database. People who answer and agree to tell us their thoughts may differ from those who don’t, and not everyone in the population might have a number in our database. Those are coverage and nonresponse problems. Alternatively, recruiting whoever walks past, volunteers online, or participates for course credit gives us a convenience sample, rather than a simple random sample of the general population. (Arguably Köbel’s churchgoers were a convenience sample; the men who attended church might not represent the broader population.)
Convenience sampling can be perfectly acceptable for some research questions, and the Central Limit Theorem still applies if treating its scores as independent observations from a common population distribution is reasonable and the sample is large enough. But generalizing beyond the population we actually sampled needs a separate argument, and increasing the sample size can’t fix a procedure that systematically produces biased data.

Summary
So to repeat and summarize, assuming we are independently sampling from a population, the distribution of sample means has an expected value, \(\mu_M\), equal to \(\mu\). It has a standard deviation, or standard error of the mean, of \(\sigma / \sqrt{n}\). Its shape is exactly normal at every \(n\) when the population is normal. For a nonnormal population, its standardized shape approaches normality gradually as \(n\) increases, at a rate that depends on the shape of the population. \(n = 30\) is often a useful convention, but it is not a magical cutoff. And we need to consider whether treating our observations as independent is reasonable, and whether the population we sampled is the one we want to make inferences about. These insights power much of the inferential statistics that we’ll move on to later, because they allow us to reason about the probability of sample statistics rather than only individual scores.

title: 8  Hypothesis Testing
text:
Spider-Man revisited
We’ll start this chapter by revisiting the idea of radioactive spider bites affecting reaction times. This time, though, we’ll move beyond one unusually quick kid and consider a whole sample of Spider-People. That will present a problem: how to decide whether our sample mean is unusual enough to count as evidence for a change in the population mean. We’ll solve it using the tools we’ve picked up over the last few chapters: \(z\)-scores, probability, sampling distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem. By putting them together, we’ll complete our first hypothesis test.
Back in Chapter 5 we considered the possibility that a radioactive spider bite might have improved the reaction times of one individual. We supposed that following the bite, our test subject, Peter Parker, had a reaction time of 189 milliseconds on a test for which the general population had a mean of 284 milliseconds and a standard deviation of 50 milliseconds. We calculated his \(z\)-score to be \(z = \frac{189 - 284}{50} = -1.9\). Assuming reaction times form a normally distributed population, we then used the unit normal table in Chapter 6 to find the proportion of scores as fast or faster than his, which turned out to be less than three percent. We decided his score seemed a bit unusual, and we wondered whether it might be evidence that the spider bite had changed his reaction time.
That thought process already contained the basic logic of a hypothesis test: we suspected the bite would cause a change, but we asked what were the chances of seeing a reaction time this fast or faster if the spider bite had done nothing. An entirely unexceptional score would give us no reason to doubt that assumption. A very unusual score would give us reason to question it.
But real research doesn’t usually rely on examining just one individual. We usually want a sample. We’d need a bunch of kids who we treated to radioactive spider bites to see if it would alter their reaction times. Obviously in the real world this experiment probably would not make it past the ethics board, but the Spiderverse™️ provides just such a scenario.
So say we find three kids, all bitten by radioactive spiders, and we measure their reaction times on the same test. Now the sample mean is 189 milliseconds. How does that change our analysis? Is it just as surprising as a single score of 189ms? More surprising? Less? Surprising enough to count as evidence that the population mean changed?

Null Hypothesis Significance Testing
Moving from one Spider-Man to a sample of Spider-People changes the calculations, but the general logic is the same. For Peter’s individual score, we used the population distribution to ask what reaction times we would commonly see if nothing had changed. For our sample mean, we’ll need the sampling distribution we learned about in Chapter 7. This describes the distribution of all possible sample means for that population and sample size. Once we know its characteristics we can ask what proportion of means are as extreme as or more extreme than the one we observed, again assuming that the spider bites didn’t change reaction times. We only test one treated sample, but we care about the hypothetical population it represents—what would happen if everyone received the treatment. The sample mean is our clue to that population mean, as Figure 8.2 illustrates.



Figure 8.2: The inferential process for a single-sample hypothesis test, from a treated sample to a conclusion about the population.




Inferential process diagram for a z test.





The formal procedure is called Null Hypothesis Significance Testing, or NHST. The spider bite is the treatment: the condition or intervention applied to our sample. A change in reaction times associated with the treatment would be a treatment effect (though a significance test alone cannot establish what caused the change).
Under NHST, as the name implies, we begin with a null hypothesis. This is a kind of skeptical working model: suppose the spider bites did nothing, so the population of bitten kids still has the same mean reaction time as the population of unbitten kids, 284 milliseconds. This becomes the null hypothesis, denoted \(H_0\). The alternative hypothesis, \(H_1\), says that the population mean changed.
For this first test, we’ll allow for a change in either direction. The null says the population mean remains 284; the alternative says it differs.
\[H_0: \mu_{\text{bitten}} = 284 \qquad H_1: \mu_{\text{bitten}} \neq 284\]
If the null is true, our three Spider-People should behave like a random sample from a population with a mean of 284. But we know that sample means vary due to sampling error, even when the population mean hasn’t changed; the sample’s mean probably won’t be exactly 284ms. So if our treated sample has a different mean, we need to judge whether the difference is more than we would typically expect from sampling error alone. We do that by imagining the sampling distribution we would get if the treatment had no effect—the null distribution—which tells us which sample means would be common and which would be unusual. Then we see where our observed mean of 189 falls.
That raises another question: how unlikely is unlikely enough? Before analyzing the data, we choose a decision criterion, called alpha and written \(\alpha\). For this first test, we’ll use \(\alpha = .05\): results in the most extreme five percent of the null distribution will count as sufficiently unusual to reject the null. (We’ll return to why we might choose that criterion and how the hypotheses determine where we place it.) We call the region defined by alpha the critical region. Its boundary is the critical value (or values, if the region is split between the two tails following a non-directional hypothesis).
There are different kinds of tests we can submit our data to, depending on the nature of the data and the information we have (or assumptions we can make) about the untreated population. In any case, we calculate a test statistic from the sample and compare it to the null distribution. If it falls in the critical region, we reject the null hypothesis; if not, we fail to reject it.
Every hypothesis test follows these four broad steps: state the hypotheses, set the decision criteria, collect and analyze the data, and make a decision. We’ll run through those steps with the Spider-People, then look back at the choices and reasoning within each one.

title: 8  Hypothesis Testing
text:
The \(z\)-test
The specific variety of test we’ll use here is called the \(z\)-test. The \(z\)-test is appropriate when we know the population standard deviation, and the sampling distribution of the mean is normal or approximately normal. As the name suggests, the test statistic is a kind of \(z\)-score:
\[z = \frac{M - \mu_0}{\sigma_M} \tag{8.1}\]
The numerator is the difference between the sample mean and the null hypothesis mean. The denominator is the standard error of the mean, which describes the variability of the null distribution. The resulting \(z\)-score tells us how many standard errors our sample mean is from the null hypothesis mean. (Compare this to the original \(z\)-scores we learned about in Chapter 5, which measured how many standard deviations an individual score was from the population mean. Same idea, applied to a different distribution.)
For this example, we’ll treat the three observations as independent and assume that, under the null, their population is normal with mean 284 and standard deviation 50. Those assumptions make the \(z\)-test appropriate here. (But note that I just made up the \(\sigma = 50\) and I told you I was taking liberties with the shape of the population. In real research, we rarely know the population standard deviation, so the \(z\)-test is not used very often. But it is a good place to start.)
Applying the full NHST \(z\)-test procedure to our Spider-Sample, the first step is to state our formal hypotheses. We’ll use a non-directional alternative hypothesis: \(H_0: \mu = 284\) and \(H_1: \mu \ne 284\).
The equations from Chapter 7 tell us that the resulting null sampling distribution has the same mean supplied by our null hypothesis (\(\mu_M = \mu_0 = 284\)) and a standard error of \(\sigma_M = \sigma / \sqrt{n} = 50 / \sqrt{3} \approx 28.87\) ms. The Central Limit Theorem tells us about its shape: if the population is normal, the sampling distribution is normal at any sample size; otherwise, it becomes approximately normal as the sample size increases. Because our sample contains only three observations, the test relies on our simplifying assumption that reaction times are normally distributed; with a large enough sample size, we could still run the \(z\)-test even if the population were skewed.
For the decision criterion, we’ll use \(\alpha = .05\). Our non-directional alternative hypothesis states that a change in either direction would count as evidence against the null. Therefore, we split that five percent between the two tails of the distribution, making this a two-tailed test. Safe in the knowledge that the sampling distribution we’re dealing with is normal, we can find the \(z\)-score that cuts off 2.5% in each tail in the unit normal table.



Table 8.1: An excerpt of the unit normal table from \(z = 1.90\) to \(z = 2.00\), highlighting the .025 upper-tail area at \(z = 1.96\) for a two-tailed test with \(\alpha = .05\).




Excerpt of the unit normal table for z from 1.90 to 2.00, with the area to the right of z = 1.96, .025, highlighted.





Since the standardized normal distribution described by the table is symmetrical, the critical values for a two-tailed test are \(z = \pm 1.96\). That means if our sample mean is more than 1.96 standard errors above or below the null mean, we will reject the null hypothesis. (Another way to think about this is that we could convert the \(\pm 1.96\) \(z\)-scores back into the original units of milliseconds, using the rearranged equation \(\mu_0 \pm z \times \sigma_M = 284 \pm 1.96 \times 28.87\), giving us critical regions below 227.4ms and above 340.6ms. If our sample mean is beyond those limits, we will reject the null hypothesis, because those are the times which put the mean’s corresponding \(z\) beyond \(\pm 1.96\).)
Next, we take our data and calculate the test statistic. First, just for comparison, recall that Peter’s individual score gave us \(z = -1.9\). That value would not be within the critical regions of the null distribution; it is less extreme than the cutoff of \(\pm 1.96\) that we obtained from Table 8.1. So now we know that Peter’s score by itself was a bit unusual, but not quite extreme enough to reject the null hypothesis, according to our stated \(\alpha = .05\).
For the sample of three, however, putting the values into the equation gives us a \(z\)-score of \(-3.29\):
\[ z = \frac{M - \mu_0}{\sigma_M} = \frac{189 - 284}{50 / \sqrt{3}} = \frac{-95}{28.87} = -3.29 \]
The numerator is the same difference we calculated for Peter alone. It’s the denominator that changes: we divide by the standard error of the mean rather than the standard deviation of individual scores.
The resulting \(z = -3.29\) for the sample of \(n = 3\) is quite a bit more extreme than \(-1.9\) for the single score, because the distribution of sample means has lower variability than the distribution of individual scores; a sample mean as far from the population mean as this is less common than an individual score that far away. Now the \(z\)-score for the sample is beyond the critical values we stated above, \(\pm 1.96\). That puts the sample mean in the lower critical region, so we would reject the null hypothesis. We call this result statistically significant at \(\alpha = .05\).
Figure 8.3 shows what the sampling distribution looks like and where our sample mean falls. I’ve included axes for both the original units (milliseconds) and the \(z\)-scores representing the sampling distribution, and shaded the critical regions red. Remember, the \(z\)-scores are just a change of label. You can see our sample mean pretty far down in the extreme tail of the distribution.



Figure 8.3: The null sampling distribution for means of \(n = 3\) reaction times, with critical regions beyond \(z = \pm 1.96\) and the observed mean of 189 ms at \(z = -3.29\).




Sampling distribution of mean reaction times for samples of three, centered on 284 ms with standard error 28.87 ms; aligned raw-score and z-score axes show the same positions, the two critical regions beyond z = ±1.96 are shaded red, and a vertical line marks the sample mean of 189 ms at z = −3.29.





In other words, if spider bites leave the population mean at 284 milliseconds, getting a sample of three people with an average of 189 milliseconds is very unlikely. The observed sample is difficult to reconcile with our assumption that the bites did nothing. That doesn’t prove what caused the difference, but it gives us evidence against the null hypothesis.

title: 8  Hypothesis Testing
text:
Hypothesis tests, step by step
Having worked through that \(z\)-test, we can scrutinize the logic and choices we made in more detail. When we learn other variations of hypothesis tests, using different statistics, the details of the calculations will change, but the general procedure will remain the same.

Step 1: State the hypotheses
We articulated two hypotheses: the null hypothesis, which we assume to be true for the purpose of the test, and the alternative hypothesis, which we will entertain if the data are inconsistent with the null. The null hypothesis usually states that there is no effect or no difference. The alternative hypothesis is usually a statement that there is an effect or a difference.
These two propositions are logical complements; one or the other must be true. But they aren’t exactly symmetric. The name of our procedure, Null Hypothesis Significance Testing, tells you that the null plays a more important role. Ronald A. Fisher, a British statistician and one of the central figures in the development of modern statistics and significance testing, stated the case bluntly: “Every experiment may be said to exist only in order to give the facts a chance of disproving the null hypothesis.” (Fisher, 1935, p. 16)
“Disproving” is overstating things a bit. A statistical result can provide quantitative evidence, but cannot establish with logical certainty that the null hypothesis is false. But Fisher’s line captures the centrality of the null. In our two-tailed example, the null supplies a specific population mean: the population mean reaction time remains exactly 284 milliseconds after a spider bite. Along with our other assumptions, that value defines a specific sampling distribution. It therefore gives us something we can check directly: if the population mean really is 284, how often would we get a sample mean this far from it or farther?
The alternative hypothesis is less specific. If the null says that the population mean is 284, the alternative just says that it is not 284. It usually doesn’t supply a particular value around which we can construct an alternative sampling distribution. So we aren’t really testing the alternative hypothesis directly; we just entertain it if the data provide sufficient evidence against the null.
A result that would be very unusual under the null gives us reason to reject it, though it doesn’t prove any specific alternative. Rejecting the null because our sample mean was 189ms doesn’t mean we’re accepting 189 as the true mean of the hypothetical population of Spider-People. We’re just saying it doesn’t seem like \(\mu_{\text{bitten}} = 284\). (We could state a specific prediction, such as \(\mu_{\text{bitten}} = 250\), giving us another sampling distribution to work with. That will be part of assessing statistical power in the next chapter. But our alternative here, \(\mu_{\text{bitten}} \neq 284\), does not make one precise numerical prediction.)
Hypotheses don’t have to concern a treatment. Say we’re interested in whether there is an association between the number of years of education someone has completed and their lifetime earnings.

General research question: Is there an association between education and income? 🎓🤑

\(H_0\): There is no association between education and income.
\(H_1\): There is an association between education and income.


Stating the alternative also means deciding whether it is directional. A directional hypothesis predicts an increase or a decrease; a non-directional hypothesis allows for a difference either way. With the spider bites, we were following the comic book logic that reaction times would be improved, so we could justify a directional hypothesis:
\[H_0: \mu_{\text{bitten}} \ge 284 \qquad H_1: \mu_{\text{bitten}} < 284\]
Here the null includes both no change and a change in the other direction. We calculate the cutoff at its boundary, \(\mu = 284\), using the same sampling distribution as before. Higher population means would make a sample mean low enough to reject the null even less likely.
But we can’t always be so sure about the direction. Perhaps in the real world radioactivity is not good for your reactions. If either change would be worth knowing about, we can use a non-directional hypothesis. Picking a direction means that even an extreme result in the other direction will not lead us to reject the null in this test. In practice, social scientists usually use non-directional hypotheses, for reasons we’ll come to in step two, where we’ll use this decision to place the critical region—or regions.
We won’t say much more about formulating hypotheses in this book. We’ll focus more on the statistical analysis used to test them. But if you really think about it, formulating our hypotheses should be by far the most important and effortful step of the entire research process. Formulating new, interesting, sensible, plausible, meaningful hypotheses isn’t easy. Even to begin to come up with reasonable and potentially insightful hypotheses requires familiarity with the existing research and theoretical perspectives on the phenomena you’re interested in, a coherent definition of the construct(s) in question, and a good sense of what makes for a good operational definition.

Step 2: Set the decision criteria
For step two, we’re asking, “if the null hypothesis is true, what sample statistics are we most likely or unlikely to see?” We already decided in step one which directions would count as evidence against the null. Now we choose how much of the null distribution will count as sufficiently unusual and put the critical region in the appropriate place. That proportion is \(\alpha\), which is also called the significance level.
A useful way to think about \(\alpha\) is that it reflects our tolerance for rejecting the null hypothesis by mistake. The sampling distribution we obtain from the null hypothesis does contain those extreme outcomes, after all; \(\alpha\) quantifies how often they would occur if we were to repeat the same experiment many times, assuming that the null is true. In other words, \(\alpha\) is the long-run probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis. Since we usually run our study just once, we can’t know whether it is one of those rare (but possible) extreme samples. Our rejection of the null is a gamble, and \(\alpha\) sets how often we are willing to lose it when the null is true.
By convention, psychology often uses an alpha level of .05. Why five percent? Ronald Fisher called it a convenient boundary in an influential 1925 statistics book, building on an older rule of thumb that results about two standard deviations from expectation were noteworthy (Fisher, 1925, pp. 47–48). Exactly two standard deviations would put \(.0228\) in each tail of the distribution, \(.0456\) total split between the two tails. So \(\alpha = .05\), or 5%, was a nice round number close to that, and you know how people like round numbers. It also caught on partly out of practicality. Textbooks often included tables for a few values of alpha rather than the whole continuous range of proportions. The convention stuck, though other thresholds can be more appropriate when the consequences of a false alarm differ.

One- and two-tailed tests
A directional hypothesis leads to a one-tailed test, with one critical region in the predicted direction. A non-directional hypothesis leads to a two-tailed test, with critical regions at both extremes. So if \(\alpha = .05\), a two-tailed test divides it between the tails, placing two and a half percent at each end of the distribution with 95% in the middle. Compare the regions in Figure 8.4.



Figure 8.4: Critical regions for \(\alpha = .05\). A one-tailed test puts all five percent in the predicted tail; a two-tailed test splits it between the two.





Standard normal curve with the lowest 5% shaded as a single critical region below z = −1.64.




Standard normal curve with two critical regions shaded, 2.5% below z = −1.96 and 2.5% above z = +1.96.






The associated critical value(s) can be found in the unit normal table, looking for the column that gives the proportion of the curve beyond a given \(z\)-score. For a one-tailed test with \(\alpha = .05\), we look for an area of about .05 in one tail:



Table 8.2: An excerpt of the unit normal table from \(z = 1.62\) to \(z = 1.67\), highlighting the .0505 upper-tail area at \(z = 1.64\) for a one-tailed test with \(\alpha = .05\).




Unit normal table excerpt: the area to the right is .0526 at z = 1.62, .0516 at 1.63, .0505 at 1.64, .0495 at 1.65, .0485 at 1.66, and .0475 at 1.67. The .0505 entry at z = 1.64 is highlighted.





In Table 8.2, at \(z = 1.64\), the area to the right is \(.0505\), or about five percent. The exact five-percent cutoff lies between \(1.64\) and \(1.65\) (about \(1.645\)), but our table gives \(z\)-scores to two decimal places. We’ll use \(1.64\) as the table-based approximation in this chapter and its quizzes. For an upper-tailed test, the cutoff is about \(+1.64\); by symmetry, for a lower-tailed test it is about \(-1.64\). For a two-tailed test, we look for .025 in each tail, giving the cutoffs of about \(\pm 1.96\) (as we found in Table 8.1).
Two-tailed tests are the default in the social sciences for the most part, even when researchers do have a hunch about the direction an effect might go in. Splitting alpha between both tails means that a result in the predicted direction has to be more extreme to reject the null: beyond \(-1.96\) rather than \(-1.64\) for a one-tailed test. So the two-tailed test is the more cautious choice, and it leaves room for an unexpected result in the other direction (like the possibility that spider bites are bad for your reaction speed, actually).
It’s also useful to stick with two-tailed tests as a default because it deters researchers from switching to a directional test after seeing the data. When we specify alpha and determine the critical regions, we’re following through on the hypotheses we stated in step one, and we’re still doing it before looking at the data. As you’ll see in Activity 8.1, it’s possible to have a result that would be significant in a one-tailed test but not in a two-tailed test. Changing the decision criteria after looking at the data would not make for a meaningful hypothesis test, any more than shooting arrows at the side of a barn and drawing a target around them afterwards would make for good target practice. Because a one-tailed test makes the null easier to reject in the predicted direction, it’s fair to be skeptical of one-tailed tests unless the direction was clearly committed to in advance.



Step 3: Collect and analyze the data
So having stated our hypotheses and decided on the decision criteria, we collect the data and calculate the appropriate sample statistics.
Again, this order of events is crucial to the logic of the hypothesis test: we’re testing how well the data fit a model specified in advance, rather than forming a model around the data we happened to find. This is sometimes called confirmatory hypothesis testing. Exploring data and noting interesting patterns can be valuable too, and those patterns can suggest new hypotheses. But that’s a different use of the data. A hypothesis suggested by the results should be treated as exploratory. To test it confirmatorily, we’d need new data.
The exact test statistic we calculate depends on the nature of the data. We’ll encounter several other tests later, including the \(t\)-test, analysis of variance (ANOVA), and correlation and regression. They all rely on the same fundamental hypothesis-testing ideas we’re outlining here. Recall that the reason we used a \(z\)-test for the Spider-People is that we assumed we knew the population standard deviation. If we didn’t want to make that assumption, we’d need a slightly different test, as we’ll see in Chapter 11.
As long as we’re talking about collecting data, allow me to remind you that the version of the Central Limit Theorem we’re using assumes independent observations drawn from the same population distribution. Random sampling is one way to support those assumptions, though in practice social scientists often collect data in less tidy ways, as we mentioned in the previous chapter.


Step 4: Make a decision
If the test statistic falls in the critical region, we reject the null hypothesis. Otherwise, we fail to reject it. That’s how we reached our decision for the Spider-People: \(z = -3.29\) was beyond the lower critical value of \(-1.96\).
There’s an equivalent way to reach the same decision, using the \(p\)-value, which we calculate from the observed data. It is the probability, assuming the null model and its other assumptions are correct, of obtaining a test statistic as extreme as or more extreme than the one we observed. For the Spider-People, it’s the probability of getting a sample mean at least as far from 284 as ours, if the null hypothesis is true.
Our Spider-Sample mean of 189ms produced a \(z\)-score of \(-3.29\). We can find the \(p\)-value associated with that score by looking it up in the unit normal table.



Table 8.3: An excerpt of the unit normal table from \(z = 3.25\) to \(z = 3.33\), highlighting the .0005 upper-tail area at \(z = 3.29\) used to find the Spider-People sample’s \(p\)-value.




Excerpt of the unit normal table for z from 3.25 to 3.33, with the area to the right of z = 3.29, .0005, highlighted.





Table 8.3 gives an area of \(.0005\) to the right of \(z = 3.29\). By symmetry, \(P(z \le -3.29) = .0005\) as well. Because our hypothesis is non-directional, an equally extreme result in the other tail also counts, giving a two-tailed \(p\)-value of approximately \(.0010\).
If \(p < \alpha\), this is another way of saying that the test statistic is in the critical region, and we reject the null hypothesis: our result is statistically significant. Here \(p \approx .001\), well below \(\alpha = .05\), so we reach the same decision as the critical-value comparison.
If \(p \ge \alpha\), we fail to reject the null hypothesis, and we call the result nonsignificant. (Not insignificant! In everyday language, “significant” suggests something large or important. Here it only indicates whether the result cleared the bar we set with \(\alpha\).) When you see \(p < .05\) in a published journal article, it usually means \(\alpha\) was chosen to be \(.05\), and the \(p\)-value for the data was less than that.
Failing to reject the null isn’t the same as accepting it or showing that nothing happened. It means this study did not provide sufficient evidence against it.
Activity 8.1 shows the decision-making process in action. We can compare how different choices would lead to different decisions with the same data, starting with our Spider-People.






Activity 8.1: Explore alpha and critical regions






Figure 8.5: How the location of the critical region, the observed \(z\)-score, and \(\alpha\) affect the decision to reject the null hypothesis.




Explore alpha and critical regions. Use the accompanying steps for an explanation.







This curve shows the null distribution of \(z\): the values we would expect if the null hypothesis is true. With \(\alpha = .05\) split between the two tails, the shaded critical regions lie beyond about \(\pm 1.96\). A result landing in either shaded region would lead us to reject the null. A result in the unshaded middle would have us fail to reject.


Now let’s add our Spider-Sample. The dashed line marks their \(z = -3.29\), well inside the lower critical region. \(p \approx .001\), which is less than \(\alpha\). The \(z\)-score falling within the critical region and \(p < \alpha\) are two ways of saying the same thing.


We could have decided on an alpha of \(.01\). The critical regions are smaller, and their boundaries move farther from zero, to about \(\pm 2.58\). The observed \(z\) and its \(p\)-value stay the same though. The decision criterion doesn’t change the evidence in the sample.


At \(\alpha = .001\), the critical values are about \(\pm 3.29\), almost exactly where our result falls. We could report the result as \(p < .001\), when that’s mathematically true, but I think it can give a misleading impression: it makes .001 look like the bar the result had to clear. If that’s what we decided in advance, fine. But if we would have been equally satisfied with \(p < .05\), we should report the actual \(p\)-value. Reporting the calculated \(p\)-value alongside the planned alpha makes the distinction clear.


Now suppose that, back in step one, we had predicted that spider bites would increase reaction times, and put all five percent in the upper tail. The result is just as extreme, but not in the direction we predicted, and we would fail to reject the null. The \(p\)-value changes to about \(.9995\), because around 99.95% of the distribution is above \(z = -3.29\).


Now consider a different sample, with \(z = -1.80\). With a two-tailed test at \(\alpha = .05\), it falls just short of the lower critical region, and \(p \approx .072\). We fail to reject the null.


Switching to a lower-tailed test moves the critical value in to about \(-1.64\). Now the same result is significant, with \(p \approx .036\)—exactly half the two-tailed value. This is why the direction has to be chosen in advance. If we pick the tail after seeing which way the result went, we would really be rejecting the null whenever \(z\) fell beyond \(\pm 1.64\) in either direction; a ten percent alpha rate disguised as five percent.

As before, the numbers are from the real study, but 30.25 and 14.89 were pre-treatment sample statistics, not known population parameters. More importantly, the means of 30.25 and 15.49 came from the same 40 people measured before and after treatment. That makes this a related-samples design, so this \(z\)-test is not the analysis we would use for the real study. We’ll return to the actual design, and the test it calls for, when we introduce the related-samples \(t\)-test in Chapter 13.

title: 8  Hypothesis Testing
text:
Summary
NHST gives us a disciplined way to ask whether a sample result is difficult to explain under a null model. But a result being significant or nonsignificant isn’t the end of the story. Determining that an effect is statistically significant doesn’t mean that it is necessarily large or of practical importance. And a nonsignificant result needn’t mean that there is no effect. To understand those possibilities, we need to look more closely at effect size, inferential errors, and statistical power, our topics for the next chapter.
Learning Checks0 of 71In our two-tailed Spider-People example, why do we assess the null
hypothesis rather than testing the alternative directly?Response optionsThe null states a specific value, which defines a specific sampling
distribution.The null is usually true, so it makes a safer starting point.The alternative can’t be stated until we’ve seen the data.Researchers usually hope that the null hypothesis is true.Show hintShow answerCheck your workClearAnswerThe null states a specific value, which defines a specific sampling
distribution.ExplanationA null such as \(\mu = 284\) gives
us one precise null distribution to compare our result against. An
alternative such as \(\mu \neq 284\)
allows for any other value, so it doesn’t give us one particular
distribution to work with.2Which of these do we need in order to use a \(z\)-test for a sample mean?Response optionsThe population standard deviation, \(\sigma\)The sample standard deviation, \(s\)A sample of at least 30 peopleA specific value for \(\mu\) under
the alternative hypothesisShow hintShow answerCheck your workClearAnswerThe population standard deviation, \(\sigma\)ExplanationThe \(z\)-test uses \(\sigma\) to calculate the standard error,
\(\sigma_M = \sigma / \sqrt{n}\).
That’s why it’s rarely used in practice. (It also needs the sampling
distribution of the mean to be normal, which a small sample only gives
us if the population itself is normal.)3Before collecting data, a researcher predicts that a treatment will
increase scores, and plans a one-tailed test with \(\alpha = .05\). What is the approximate
critical value, using this chapter’s table?Response options\(z = +1.64\)\(z = -1.64\)\(z = +1.96\)\(z = \pm 1.96\)Show hintShow answerCheck your workClearAnswer\(z = +1.64\)ExplanationAll five percent goes in the predicted tail, and an increase means
the upper tail. The table gives an upper-tail area of .0505 at \(z = +1.64\), our approximation for the
five-percent cutoff. The values \(\pm
1.96\) leave .025 in each tail, which is what a two-tailed test
needs.4A study reports \(p = .03\). What
does that mean?Response optionsIf the null were true, a result at least this extreme would happen
about 3% of the time.There is a 3% chance that the null hypothesis is true.There is a 97% chance that the alternative hypothesis is true.There is a 3% chance that the researchers made the wrong
decision.Show hintShow answerCheck your workClearAnswerIf the null were true, a result at least this extreme would happen
about 3% of the time.ExplanationA \(p\)-value is calculated by
assuming the null is true. So it can’t also tell us the
probability that the null is true. It tells us how unusual our result
would be in a world where the null hypothesis holds.5A researcher sets \(\alpha = .05\).
What does that five percent describe?Response optionsHow often, in the long run, we would reject the null when it is
actually trueThe probability that the null hypothesis is trueThe probability that this particular rejection of the null is a
mistakeThe proportion of the sample’s scores that fall in the critical
regionShow hintShow answerCheck your workClearAnswerHow often, in the long run, we would reject the null when it is
actually trueExplanationIf the null is true, five percent of possible results still land in
the critical region, so a researcher who uses \(\alpha = .05\) will reject a true null
about five percent of the time. For any one study, though, we can’t know
whether it was one of those unlucky samples.6A result is statistically significant at \(\alpha = .05\). What does that tell us?Response optionsThe result fell in the critical region, so \(p < .05\).The effect is large enough to matter in practice.The null hypothesis has been proven false.The treatment caused the difference.Show hintShow answerCheck your workClearAnswerThe result fell in the critical region, so \(p < .05\).Explanation“Significant” only means that the result cleared the bar we set with
\(\alpha\). It doesn’t mean the effect
is big or important, it doesn’t prove the null false, and a significance
test alone can’t establish what caused the difference.7A study produces \(p = .12\), with
\(\alpha = .05\). What is the
appropriate conclusion?Response optionsFail to reject the null; this study didn’t provide sufficient
evidence against it.Accept the null; the treatment had no effect.There is a 12% chance that the null hypothesis is true.The result is insignificant, so any effect is too small to
matter.Show hintShow answerCheck your workClearAnswerFail to reject the null; this study didn’t provide sufficient
evidence against it.ExplanationSince \(p > \alpha\), we fail to
reject the null. But that doesn’t show the null is true: a real effect
might have been missed. The \(p\)-value
isn’t the probability that the null is true. And “nonsignificant” isn’t
a verdict about how big or important an effect is.
